blocks.text:
Software that runs correctly on a developer laptop frequently fails on a server because the two machines differ in operating system packages, library versions, environment variables, file layout or Java runtime. Installing the application directly on a shared host also couples every application on that host to the same libraries and the same failure domain. A virtual machine removes these problems at a high cost: every instance carries a complete guest operating system, so each one consumes memory and disk for a kernel and a userland that are not part of the application.

A container solves the same problem with a different mechanism. The application, together with the exact userland it needs, is packaged as an image and started as an ordinary Linux process whose view of the system is restricted by the kernel. No second kernel is booted. The consequences are fast start-up, high density per host and an identical runtime environment from laptop to production. The trade-off is a weaker isolation boundary than a virtual machine, because all containers on a host share one kernel.

This chapter explains the two kernel features that create the illusion of a separate machine, namespaces and control groups, and demonstrates each of them with commands that run on any Linux host. The Spring Boot guides already cover how an application is built and run; this Part covers how it is packaged and operated as a container. The `orders-service` application (Spring Boot 3, Java 21, Maven, PostgreSQL) is the running example.

### Concept and mechanism

#### What a container is

A container is a process, or a tree of processes, started with three restrictions applied by the Linux kernel:

- a restricted view of kernel resources (process IDs, network interfaces, mount points, host name), provided by **namespaces**;
- a restricted quantity of CPU, memory and process slots, enforced by **control groups** (cgroups);
- a private root file system, assembled from the read-only layers of an image plus one writable layer (covered in the next chapter).

There is no kernel object called a container. The container runtime creates the namespaces and cgroups, mounts the root file system and starts the process. This has a practical consequence: a Linux container needs a Linux kernel. Docker Desktop on macOS and Windows therefore runs a small Linux virtual machine and starts the containers inside it.

blocks.text:
The two technologies are complementary. Cloud providers commonly run containers inside virtual machines, which combines the packaging benefits of containers with the stronger tenant isolation of a hypervisor.

#### Namespaces

A **namespace** wraps a global kernel resource so that processes inside the namespace see their own private instance of it. Linux provides these namespaces, each created by a flag of the `clone` or `unshare` system call.

rows: Process ID numbering; the first process becomes PID 1
Network interfaces, routing table, ports, firewall rules
The mount table and therefore the visible file system tree
System V IPC objects and POSIX message queues
User and group ID mappings (root inside, unprivileged outside)
The view of the cgroup hierarchy
blocks.caption: Linux namespaces used by container runtimes.

blocks.text:
Every process belongs to exactly one namespace of each type. The memberships are visible as symbolic links in `/proc/PID/ns`, and two processes share a namespace when the link targets (inode numbers) are equal.

#### Control groups

A **control group** is a kernel hierarchy that groups processes and applies accounting and limits to the group. A controller manages one resource: `memory` limits RAM, `cpu` limits CPU time by quota, `pids` limits the number of processes, `blkio` or `io` weights disk I/O. The runtime creates one cgroup per container and writes the limits requested with `docker run` into control files in that directory.

Two layouts exist. Version 1 uses one hierarchy per controller (`/sys/fs/cgroup/memory/...`, `/sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/...`). Version 2 uses a single unified hierarchy with files such as `memory.max`, `cpu.max` and `pids.max`. The build machine used for this guide runs cgroup version 1 (`docker info` reports `Cgroup Version: 1`), so file names below are the version 1 names; modern distributions default to version 2 and the concepts are identical.

blocks.text:
### Worked example

All commands in this section were executed on the build machine as root. Identifiers such as namespace inode numbers differ on every boot.

#### Namespaces with unshare

The `unshare` utility runs a command in new namespaces without any container runtime. The first example creates a PID namespace and remounts `/proc` so that the process list matches the new namespace.

blocks.code:
$ unshare --pid --fork --mount-proc bash -c 'echo "inside: pid=$$"; ps -e -o pid,comm'
inside: pid=1
    PID COMMAND
      1 ps
blocks.title: PID namespace

blocks.text: The shell reports PID 1 and no other process is visible, although the host is running many. In a UTS namespace the host name can be changed without affecting the host:

blocks.code:
$ unshare --uts bash -c 'hostname v2-demo; hostname'
v2-demo
$ hostname
vm
blocks.title: UTS namespace

blocks.text: A network namespace starts with only a loopback interface, whereas the host has several:

blocks.code:
$ unshare --net bash -c 'cat /proc/net/dev | tail -n +3 | cut -d: -f1'
    lo
$ cat /proc/net/dev | tail -n +3 | cut -d: -f1 | tr '\n' ' '
    lo   ifb0   ifb1   eth0 br-9dfe55f427a7
blocks.title: Network namespace

blocks.text: A mount namespace isolates mounts. A tmpfs mounted inside the namespace is invisible to the host:

blocks.code:
$ unshare --mount bash -c 'mount -t tmpfs none /tmp/demo; touch /tmp/demo/x; ls /tmp/demo'
x
$ echo "host sees: [$(ls /tmp/demo)]"
host sees: []
blocks.title: Mount namespace

blocks.text: A user namespace maps an unprivileged user to root inside the namespace. The mapping file shows that UID 0 inside corresponds to a single host UID:

blocks.code:
$ unshare --user --map-root-user bash -c 'id; cat /proc/self/uid_map'
uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)
         0          0          1
blocks.title: User namespace

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Build environment. The Docker daemon used for every demonstration in this Part has no internet access and cannot pull images. Base images were therefore created locally with `docker import` from a tar archive of a minimal root file system (bash, core utilities, shared libraries, and for the Java images a JDK 21 and a runtime produced by `jlink`). Image names are prefixed `v2-`. Behaviour of the kernel, daemon and Dockerfile builder is genuine; the contents of the base images differ from the official ones such as `eclipse-temurin`.

#### Limits with cgroups

A container with all three limits was started and the control files were read from the host:

blocks.code:
$ docker run -d --name v2-lim --network none --memory 64m --memory-swap 64m \
    --cpus 0.5 --pids-limit 20 v2-base:1 sleep 300
$ ID=$(docker inspect -f '{{.Id}}' v2-lim); C=/sys/fs/cgroup
$ cat $C/memory/docker/$ID/memory.limit_in_bytes
67108864
$ cat $C/cpu/docker/$ID/cpu.cfs_period_us $C/cpu/docker/$ID/cpu.cfs_quota_us
100000
50000
$ cat $C/pids/docker/$ID/pids.max
20
blocks.title: Limits written into the cgroup

blocks.text:
The value 67108864 is 64 x 1024 x 1024. The option `--cpus 0.5` becomes a quota of 50000 microseconds of CPU time in every 100000 microsecond period.

Exceeding the process limit makes `fork` fail. A container started with `--pids-limit 20` tried to start 30 background processes:

blocks.code:
$ docker exec v2-lim bash -c 'for ((i=0;i<30;i++)); do sleep 100 & done'
bash: fork: retry: Resource temporarily unavailable
bash: fork: retry: Resource temporarily unavailable
bash: fork: Resource temporarily unavailable
$ cat $C/pids/docker/$ID/pids.current $C/pids/docker/$ID/pids.max
19
20
blocks.title: pids limit reached (typical output)

blocks.text: CPU limits throttle instead of killing. A container running an infinite loop under `--cpus 0.5` was observed for five seconds:

blocks.code:
$ docker run -d --name v2-cpu --network none --cpus 0.5 v2-base:1 bash -c 'while :; do :; done'
$ cat $C/cpu/docker/$ID/cpu.stat
nr_periods 53
nr_throttled 50
throttled_time 2403006398
$ docker stats --no-stream --format '{{.Name}} CPU={{.CPUPerc}}'
v2-cpu CPU=50.73%
blocks.title: CPU throttling

blocks.text:
The process was runnable in every period but was paused by the scheduler in 50 of 53 periods, so it consumed half of one CPU. `throttled_time` is in nanoseconds (about 2.4 seconds here).

Memory limits kill. A C program that allocates and touches memory in 1 MiB steps was run under a 64 MiB limit with swap disabled (`--memory-swap` equal to `--memory`):

blocks.code:
$ docker run --name v2-oom --network none --memory 64m --memory-swap 64m v2-base:1 hog 200
allocated 16 MiB
allocated 32 MiB
allocated 48 MiB
$ echo $?
137
$ docker inspect -f 'OOMKilled={{.State.OOMKilled}} ExitCode={{.State.ExitCode}}' v2-oom
OOMKilled=true ExitCode=137
blocks.title: Memory limit exceeded

blocks.text:
The kernel OOM killer sent SIGKILL (signal 9); the exit code is 128 + 9 = 137. The program printed no error because it never had the chance to run any handler.

#### A cgroup without Docker

The same mechanism is available directly. A memory cgroup was created by hand, the current shell was moved into it and the same program was started:

blocks.code:
$ mkdir /sys/fs/cgroup/memory/v2demo
$ echo 33554432 > /sys/fs/cgroup/memory/v2demo/memory.limit_in_bytes
$ echo 33554432 > /sys/fs/cgroup/memory/v2demo/memory.memsw.limit_in_bytes
$ bash -c 'echo $$ > /sys/fs/cgroup/memory/v2demo/cgroup.procs; /tmp/dvw_v2/hog 100'
allocated 16 MiB
/bin/bash: line 28:  5378 Killed                  bash -c '...'
$ rmdir /sys/fs/cgroup/memory/v2demo
blocks.title: Manual cgroup (cgroup v1 paths)

blocks.text:
The program was killed before reaching 32 MiB, which confirms that a container runtime adds convenience and bookkeeping to kernel features but no isolation mechanism of its own.

### Hands-on

Objective: observe PID, UTS and mount isolation and a memory limit on any Linux host with root access (a virtual machine or WSL 2 is sufficient).

1. Run `unshare --pid --fork --mount-proc bash` and execute `ps -e`. Confirm that the shell is PID 1. Exit the shell.
2. Run `unshare --uts bash`, change the host name with `hostname lab`, print it, exit, and confirm that the host name outside is unchanged.
3. Run `ls -l /proc/self/ns` in two terminals and compare the inode numbers; then repeat inside `unshare --net` `bash` and note which entry changes.
4. If Docker is installed, start `docker run -d --name lab --memory 64m alpine sleep 300` (any small image), read `/sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max` (cgroup v2) or `/sys/fs/cgroup/memory/docker/ID/memory.limit_in_bytes` (cgroup v1) and compare it with 64 MiB expressed in bytes.
5. Remove the container with `docker rm -f lab`.

Expected result: PID 1 in step 1, a changed host name only inside step 2, differing inode numbers for `net` in step 3 and the value 67108864 in step 4.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem 1: container disappears with exit code 137 and no error in the log

**Scenario.** A batch job container processes a large file. It runs for a few minutes and then stops.

**Symptoms.** `docker ps -a` shows `Exited (137)`. `docker logs` ends abruptly with no exception or stack trace.

**Diagnosis.** `docker inspect -f '{{.State.OOMKilled}}' NAME` prints `true`. On the host, `dmesg` contains a line of the form "Memory cgroup out of memory: Killed process". Exit code 137 is 128 plus signal 9.

**Root cause.** The total memory of the container (heap, native memory, page cache attributed to the cgroup) exceeded the `--memory` limit and the kernel OOM killer terminated the process. The process had no opportunity to log.

**Fix.** Raise the limit, or reduce the memory consumption (stream the file instead of loading it, set an explicit heap smaller than the limit for a JVM, see the chapter on Spring Boot containers).

**Prevention.** Set memory limits deliberately, monitor `docker stats` during load tests, and alert on `OOMKilled` restarts.

#### Problem 2: service becomes slow under a CPU limit without any error

**Scenario.** The `orders-service` container is started with `--cpus 0.5` to share a host. Latency rises sharply under load.

**Symptoms.** CPU usage stays at about 50 percent in `docker stats` although the request queue grows. No restarts occur.

**Diagnosis.** In the container cgroup, `cpu.stat` shows `nr_throttled` close to `nr_periods`, which means the process is paused in most scheduling periods.

**Root cause.** A CFS quota caps CPU time per 100 ms period. A multi-threaded application that needs bursts of CPU exhausts the quota early in each period and is then suspended until the next period.

**Fix.** Increase the limit or use CPU shares (`--cpu-shares`, a relative weight) when strict capping is not required.

**Prevention.** Load test with the intended limits and check throttling counters before production.

### Questions to expect

**Q1. What is the difference between a container and a virtual machine?** A virtual machine runs a full guest operating system with its own kernel on virtualised hardware. A container is a process on the host kernel, isolated by namespaces and limited by cgroups. Containers start faster and use less memory, but share the kernel and therefore have a weaker isolation boundary.

**Q2. Which Linux features implement containers?** Namespaces (pid, net, mnt, uts, ipc, user, cgroup) restrict what a process can see. Control groups restrict what it can consume. A layered root file system (overlayfs) provides the image content. Capabilities and seccomp profiles further restrict system calls.

**Q3. What does PID 1 inside a container correspond to on the host?** It is the same process with a different PID. The host sees it under its host PID (for example 4232) and the container sees it as 1 because of the PID namespace.

**Q4. How does Docker enforce** `--memory 512m`**?** The runtime writes the limit into the container memory cgroup (`memory.limit_in_bytes` in v1, `memory.max` in v2). When usage cannot be reclaimed below the limit the kernel OOM killer sends SIGKILL, producing exit code 137 and `OOMKilled=true`.

**Q5. How do memory limits and CPU limits differ in effect?** Memory is an incompressible resource: exceeding it kills the process. CPU is compressible: exceeding the quota throttles the process.

**Q6. Why does a Linux container not run natively on macOS?** Containers use Linux kernel features. Docker Desktop starts a Linux virtual machine and runs the containers inside it.

**Q7. Is root inside a container the same as root on the host?** By default yes: UID 0 maps to host UID 0 because the user namespace is shared. Capabilities are reduced, but a kernel or configuration flaw can expose the host. Running as a non-root user or enabling user-namespace remapping or rootless mode reduces the risk. **Q8. How can the namespaces of a running process be inspected?** List `/proc/PID/ns`; equal inode numbers mean a shared namespace. `lsns` and `nsenter -t PID` provide the same information and entry into a namespace.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- A container is an ordinary process restricted by namespaces (visibility), cgroups (resources) and a layered root file system; there is no second kernel.
- Docker creates new pid, net, mnt, uts and ipc namespaces by default; cgroup and user namespaces are shared with the host.
- Memory limits kill (exit 137, OOMKilled), CPU limits throttle, pids limits make fork fail.
- All kernel features used by Docker can be exercised directly with unshare and /sys/fs/cgroup.
- Shared-kernel isolation is weaker than a hypervisor boundary; harden containers accordingly.

An application is delivered as an image: an immutable bundle containing a root file system and the default command. Understanding what an image physically consists of explains three practical matters: why pushes and pulls transfer only some data, why tags are unreliable identifiers while digests are exact, and why the order of instructions in a Dockerfile decides how long every build takes.

### Concept and mechanism

An OCI image is made of three kinds of objects, each stored as a blob and identified by the SHA-256 hash of its bytes (a **digest**, written `sha256:` followed by 64 hexadecimal digits):

- the **manifest**, a small JSON document that lists the configuration blob and the layer blobs;
- the **configuration**, a JSON document with the architecture and operating system, default environment, entrypoint and command, working directory, exposed ports, the **history** (one entry per Dockerfile instruction) and `rootfs.diff_ids`, the digests of the uncompressed layer tarballs;
- the **layers**, each a tar archive (usually gzip-compressed) containing the files added, modified or whiteout-deleted by one filesystem-changing instruction.

An **image index** (also called a manifest list) may sit above several manifests, one per platform, so that one name resolves to the right image on amd64 and arm64 hosts.

blocks.text:
Two digests exist per layer because compression changes the bytes. The manifest refers to the compressed blob, which is what travels over the network. The configuration's `diff_ids` refer to the uncompressed tarball, which identifies the layer content on disk regardless of compression.

#### Layers, copy-on-write and size

Only instructions that change the file system create layers with content: `RUN`, `COPY`, `ADD`. Instructions such as `ENV`, `EXPOSE`, `ENTRYPOINT` and `LABEL` change only the configuration and create history entries marked as empty layers. Layers are additive: deleting a file in a later layer hides it but does not shrink the image, because the earlier layer still contains the bytes (this is the root of the secrets-in-layers problem treated later).

#### Tags and digests

A **tag** such as `orders-service:1.4.2` is a mutable pointer maintained by the registry; the same tag can later point to different content. A **digest** reference such as `orders-service@sha256:...` always resolves to exactly the same bytes. Production deployments that need reproducibility pin digests or use tags that are never reassigned.

#### The build cache

Each Dockerfile instruction in a build is a cache candidate. BuildKit reuses a stored result when the parent step was reused, the instruction text is the same and, for `COPY` and `ADD`, the checksum of the source files is the same. For `RUN`, only the command text is compared, not the effect of the command: a `RUN` that downloads dependencies is considered unchanged even when the remote content changed. The first instruction that misses the cache forces every later instruction to execute again.

### Worked example

The application is a small C program (`main.c`) that links a helper library (`lib.c`), built in a first stage that has a compiler and copied into a `scratch` image. The multi-stage syntax is explained in the chapter on Dockerfiles; here it serves as a real, fast build.

blocks.code:
FROM v2-builder:1 AS build
WORKDIR /build
COPY lib.h lib.c ./
RUN gcc -c -O2 lib.c -o lib.o
COPY main.c ./
RUN gcc -static -O2 main.c lib.o -o app

FROM scratch
COPY --from=build /build/app /app
ENTRYPOINT ["/app"]

blocks.text: (The first build shows `WORKDIR` as `ran`; in an earlier experiment on the same daemon it had been cached, which is consistent with content-based caching.) Editing `main.c` invalidates from `COPY main.c` onward; editing `lib.c` invalidates from the first `COPY`. A second Dockerfile that begins with `COPY . .` illustrates the contrasting order:

blocks.code:
$ docker build -f Dockerfile.bad -t v2-cachebad:1 .
CACHED  [build 2/5] WORKDIR /build
ran     [build 3/5] COPY . .
ran     [build 4/5] RUN gcc -c -O2 lib.c -o lib.o
ran     [build 5/5] RUN gcc -static -O2 main.c lib.o -o app
CACHED  [stage-1 1/1] COPY --from=build /build/app /app
blocks.title: Same project, COPY . . first, after editing only README.md

blocks.text: README.md is part of the copied context, so its checksum changed and both compile steps ran again although no code changed. The last step was `CACHED` because the compiled binary was byte-identical, which shows that `COPY --from` is keyed on the content of the source files. With the layered Dockerfile the same README edit produced `CACHED` on every step.

blocks.text:
### Hands-on

Objective: observe layer caching and inspect an image archive.

1. Create a directory with `hello.c` (prints one line), a `Dockerfile` that compiles it in a build stage and copies the static binary into `FROM scratch`, and a `README.md`.
2. Build twice with `docker build --progress=plain -t lab:1 .` and confirm that the second build reports `CACHED` for all steps.
3. Edit `README.md` and rebuild. Move `COPY README.md .` to be the last instruction before the final stage if it is needed at all, or exclude it with `.dockerignore`, and rebuild to see the effect.
4. Run `docker history lab:1`, then `docker save lab:1 -o lab.tar`, extract it and print `manifest.json`.
5. Verify a layer digest with `sha256sum` of the layer blob.

Expected result: the second build is fully cached; the layer file name equals its SHA-256.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem 5: image is far larger than the application

**Scenario.** A Java service of a few kilobytes of classes is delivered as an image of hundreds of megabytes.

**Symptoms.** Pushes and pulls are slow and registry storage grows quickly.

**Diagnosis.** `docker history IMAGE` lists the size per instruction. On the build machine the single-stage image of the demo application (compiled and run on a full JDK base) measured 335 MB, whereas the multi-stage image with a `jlink` runtime measured 95.3 MB as reported by `docker images`. The C demonstration measured 283 MB against 1.14 MB. The large rows are the base image and the toolchain.

**Root cause.** Build tools (compiler, headers, package caches) remained in the final image, and the base contained a full JDK where a runtime would do.

**Fix.** Use a multi-stage build, a smaller runtime base, and remove package-manager caches in the same `RUN` that creates them (a later `rm` does not shrink earlier layers).

**Prevention.** Review `docker history` in code review and add an image size budget to the pipeline.

#### Problem 6: build cache never hits

**Scenario.** Every pipeline run downloads all Maven dependencies although only one class changed.

**Symptoms.** The dependency step shows the full duration in every build log.

**Diagnosis.** In the log the `COPY . .` step precedes `RUN mvn dependency:go-offline`; any changed file invalidates it. On a fresh CI runner the local cache is also empty at the start of the job.

**Root cause.** The cache key of `COPY` includes the checksums of all copied files, so an early, broad `COPY` invalidates all later steps. Ephemeral CI runners start without a cache.

**Fix.** Copy `pom.xml` first, resolve dependencies, then copy `src`. Add a `.dockerignore`. On ephemeral runners export and import the cache (`--cache-to` and `--cache-from` with a registry or local cache backend).

**Prevention.** Order instructions from least to most frequently changing and measure cache hit rates.

### Questions to expect

**Q1. What is an image layer?** A tar archive of file-system changes produced by one instruction (`RUN`, `COPY`, `ADD`). Layers are read-only, content-addressed and shared between images and containers.

**Q2. What is the difference between a tag and a digest?** A tag is a movable name; a digest is the SHA-256 of the manifest and cannot refer to different content. Pinning a digest guarantees identical bytes.

**Q3. Why does deleting a file in a later** `RUN` **not reduce the image size?** Layers are additive. The earlier layer still stores the file; the later layer adds only a whiteout.

**Q4. How does the Docker build cache decide whether to reuse a step?** If the parent was reused, the instruction text is identical and, for `COPY` and `ADD`, the file checksums are identical. A miss invalidates all following steps.

**Q5. Why are there both a digest of the layer in the manifest and** `diff_ids` **in the config?** The manifest digest is over the compressed blob transferred by the registry; the `diff_id` is over the uncompressed tar and identifies the content independent of compression.

**Q6. Which instructions create layers with content?** `RUN`, `COPY` and `ADD`. Instructions that only set metadata create empty history entries.

**Q7. What is an image index?** A manifest list that maps platforms (os/architecture) to manifests so that one name works on several architectures.

**Q8. How are layers shared on disk?** By digest: identical layers are stored once, and containers started from one image share the read-only layers and each adds its own writable layer.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- An image is a manifest, a configuration and layer tarballs, all addressed by SHA-256 digests.
- Tags move; digests do not. Pin digests when reproducibility matters.
- Layers are additive: removing a file later never reduces size.
- The cache invalidates from the first changed step onward; order instructions from stable to volatile.
- docker history, docker image inspect and docker save show the real structure of an image.

A Dockerfile is a text file of instructions from which `docker build` produces an image. It is the executable specification of the runtime environment of an application, so its quality determines build time, image size, start-up behaviour, shutdown behaviour and security. A Dockerfile that merely works on the first attempt commonly produces images that rebuild slowly, ignore termination signals and run as root. This chapter presents each instruction, the rules that make builds fast and containers well behaved, and a complete image that was built and run on the build machine.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Instruction reference

rows: Selects the base image; starts a build stage (`FROM base AS` `name`)
Sets the working directory for following instructions and the container; creates it if absent
Copies files from the build context (or from another stage with `--from`) into the image
Like COPY, and additionally extracts local tar archives and accepts URLs
Executes a command in a temporary container and stores the file-system changes
Sets an environment variable in the image and in every container
Declares a build-time variable, available only while building
Documents the port the application listens on; does not publish it
Sets the user (and group) for following instructions and the container process
Default arguments for ENTRYPOINT, or the default command
Command the daemon runs periodically to determine the container health
Adds key-value metadata (OCI annotations such as `org.opencontainers.image.source`)
blocks.caption: Dockerfile instructions used in practice.

blocks.text:
Each instruction is explained further where it carries a pitfall.

#### COPY compared with ADD

Use `COPY` by default. `ADD` also unpacks local tar archives and fetches remote URLs, which hides behaviour: an archive is extracted without being requested, and a URL source gives no checksum guarantee unless one is supplied. Use `ADD` only when automatic extraction of a local archive is wanted.

#### ENV compared with ARG

`ARG` exists only during the build; `ENV` persists into the image and every container. The following Dockerfile and runs were executed on the build machine:

blocks.code:
FROM v2-base:1
ARG BUILD_VERSION=dev
ENV APP_MODE=prod
RUN echo "building ${BUILD_VERSION}" > /tmp/build.txt
CMD ["bash", "-c", "echo mode=$APP_MODE version=[$BUILD_VERSION]; cat /tmp/build.txt"]
blocks.title: Dockerfile

blocks.code:
$ docker build --build-arg BUILD_VERSION=1.4.2 -t v2-envarg:1 .
$ docker run --rm v2-envarg:1
mode=prod version=[]
building 1.4.2
$ docker run --rm -e APP_MODE=test v2-envarg:1
mode=test version=[]
building 1.4.2
$ docker image inspect v2-envarg:1 --format '{{.Config.Env}}'
[PATH=/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin APP_MODE=prod]
blocks.title: ARG is build-time only, ENV is runtime

blocks.text:
The build argument was visible to `RUN` but empty at run time; the `ENV` value was present and overridable with `-e`. A build argument is not a secret store: its value is recorded in the image history (demonstrated in the chapter on container security).

#### ENTRYPOINT, CMD and the two command forms

`ENTRYPOINT` defines the program; `CMD` supplies default arguments that `docker run IMAGE ARGS` replaces. Both exist in two forms.

- **Exec form**, a JSON array: `ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "/app/app.jar"]`. The program is started directly and becomes PID 1.
- **Shell form**, a plain string: `ENTRYPOINT java -jar /app/app.jar`. Docker runs `/bin/sh -c "..."`, so the shell is PID 1 and the program is its child, unless the shell replaces itself with the program.

PID 1 has special properties in Linux: the kernel does not apply the default action for signals it has no handler for. A process that is PID 1 and installs no SIGTERM handler ignores SIGTERM. `docker stop` sends SIGTERM, waits 10 seconds by default and then sends SIGKILL. An application that is not PID 1 never receives the signal at all when the PID 1 shell does not forward it.

Three variants of the demonstration image (a Java HTTP server that registers a shutdown hook, described in the next chapter) were started and stopped on the build machine:

blocks.code:
#!/bin/bash
echo "wrapper: starting"
java -jar /app/orders-lite.jar
echo "wrapper: java returned"

blocks.text: The shell-form result needs a qualification. On the build machine `/bin/sh` is bash, which executes a single simple command in `sh -c` without forking, so the program became PID 1. The default `/bin/sh` of Debian and Ubuntu (dash) and of Alpine (BusyBox ash) can behave differently, and any shell form with several commands, pipes or `&&` keeps the shell as PID 1. The exec form does not depend on the shell and is the reliable choice. Exit code 143 is 128 plus 15 (SIGTERM) and indicates that the JVM terminated through its signal handling.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: Scripts that prepare configuration and then start the application must end with `exec java ...` (or `exec "$@"`). For programs that cannot handle signals, `docker run --init` (or `init: true` in Compose) starts a tiny init process (`docker-init`, version 0.19.0 on the build machine) that forwards signals and reaps zombie processes.

#### USER

Containers run as root unless a user is set. Creating an unprivileged user and switching to it limits the damage of a compromised process (see the chapter on container security). Use a numeric UID, which works even when the image has no user database entry and is understood by Kubernetes policies such as `runAsNonRoot`. Files that the application must write need matching ownership, which is also the source of the bind-mount permission problem treated in the chapter on runtime and storage.

#### HEALTHCHECK

`HEALTHCHECK` stores a command that the daemon runs inside the container at an interval. Exit status 0 marks the container healthy, 1 unhealthy. Options are `--interval`, `--timeout`, `--start-period` (failures during start-up are not counted) and `--retries`. Defaults of 30 s, 30 s, 0 s and 3 are from memory of the reference; verify against the Dockerfile reference before relying on them. The status appears in `docker ps` and in `docker inspect`:

blocks.code:
$ docker run -d --name v2-hc --health-cmd 'false' --health-interval 1s --health-retries 2 \
    v2-base:1 sleep 60
$ docker inspect -f '{{.State.Health.Status}} failing={{.State.Health.FailingStreak}}' v2-hc
unhealthy failing=4
blocks.title: A failing health command

blocks.text:
Docker itself only reports the status; it does not restart an unhealthy container. Orchestrators and Compose (`depends_on` with `condition: service_healthy`) act on it. The command must exist inside the image: a minimal image without `curl` needs a different probe (the demonstration image uses a bash `/dev/tcp` script).

#### .dockerignore

The build context is the directory sent to the daemon. A `.dockerignore` file excludes paths from it, which speeds up the transfer, keeps secrets and `.git` out of the image and prevents irrelevant changes from invalidating `COPY` steps. A typical file for the Maven service lists `target/`, `.git`, `.idea/`, `*.iml`, `.env`, and `Dockerfile` itself is not required to be listed.

#### Multi-stage builds

A Dockerfile may contain several `FROM` instructions. Each starts a stage; `COPY --from=NAME` takes files from an earlier stage. The final stage contains only what it copies, so compilers and build caches stay behind. The measured effect on the build machine (sizes as reported by `docker images`):

blocks.text:
### Worked example

The `orders-service-lite` image stands in for the Spring Boot service, because Maven dependencies cannot be downloaded on the build machine. It is a single Java source file using the JDK built-in HTTP server: `/actuator/health` reports `UP` when a TCP connection to the database host from `SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL` succeeds and `DOWN` otherwise; `/orders` returns a fixed list; `/alloc?mb=N` allocates heap for memory experiments; a shutdown hook prints a message. The Dockerfile follows the same structure as a production one:

blocks.code:
FROM v2-jdk:21 AS build
WORKDIR /build
COPY src/ src/
RUN mkdir out \
 && javac -d out src/OrdersLite.java \
 && jar --create --file orders-lite.jar --main-class OrdersLite -C out .

FROM v2-jre:21
LABEL org.opencontainers.image.title="orders-service-lite" \
      org.opencontainers.image.source="https://example.com/orders-service"
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /build/orders-lite.jar /app/orders-lite.jar
COPY healthcheck.sh /app/healthcheck.sh
ENV SERVER_PORT=8080
EXPOSE 8080
USER 10001:10001
HEALTHCHECK --interval=5s --timeout=3s --start-period=5s --retries=3 CMD ["/app/healthcheck.sh"]
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "/app/orders-lite.jar"]
blocks.title: Dockerfile

blocks.text:
What to notice:

- `v2-jdk:21` and `v2-jre:21` are locally imported bases standing in for a JDK and a JRE image; the build stage compiles, and only the jar reaches the final stage.
- The whole `RUN` is one instruction so that one layer results (several commands joined with `&&`).
- `EXPOSE` documents the port; publishing is done at run time with `-p`.
- `USER 10001:10001` and the exec-form `ENTRYPOINT` follow the rules above.

The image was built and started without network access:

$ docker build --network none --provenance=false -t v2-orders:1 .

blocks.text: Variables expand in `ENTRYPOINT` and `CMD` only in the shell form. In the exec form, `["java", "-jar", "$APP_JAR"]` passes the literal string `$APP_JAR`. Use `["sh", "-c", "exec java $JAVA_OPTS -jar app.jar"]` when expansion is required, and keep `exec` in it.

### Hands-on

Objective: build the layer-friendly image of a small program and verify signal handling.

1. Write a program that prints a line, sleeps in a loop and prints a message when it receives SIGTERM (a shell script with `trap 'echo stopping; exit 0' TERM` is sufficient).
2. Create two Dockerfiles: one with `CMD ./app.sh` and one with `ENTRYPOINT ["./app.sh"]`.
3. Run each with `docker run -d --name t IMAGE`, then execute `docker exec t ps -e` and `time docker stop t`.
4. Add a wrapper `start.sh` that calls the script without `exec` and observe the stop time; then add `exec`.
5. Add `HEALTHCHECK CMD test -f /tmp/ready` and create the file with `docker exec t touch /tmp/ready`; watch `docker ps` change from `(health: starting)` to `(healthy)`.

Expected result: the stop time is about 0.1 s when the script is PID 1 and handles the signal, and about 10 s when a wrapper shell is PID 1 without exec.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem 7: container exits immediately

**Scenario.** A container based on a shell image is started with `docker run -d` and is not found afterwards.

**Symptoms.** `docker ps` is empty; `docker ps -a` lists the container as `Exited (0)` a second after the start. `docker logs` prints nothing.

blocks.code:
$ docker run -d --name v2-ex v2-base:1 bash
$ docker ps -a --filter name=v2-ex --format '{{.Names}} {{.Status}}'
v2-ex Exited (0) 1 second ago
blocks.title: Observed on the build machine

blocks.text:
**Diagnosis.** The status and exit code show that the main process finished by itself. An interactive shell ends immediately when standard input is closed, which is the case without `-it`. For servers, the same symptom appears when the command starts a daemon that forks into the background so that PID 1 returns.

**Root cause.** A container lives exactly as long as its PID 1 process. When PID 1 exits, the container stops.

**Fix.** Run the foreground process of the application (`java -jar ...`), keep a shell alive only when needed with `-it`, and configure daemons to stay in the foreground.

**Prevention.** Define `ENTRYPOINT` in the image so that the intended process is PID 1, and test the image with `docker` `run` before pushing it.

#### Problem 8: container takes ten seconds to stop and exits with 137

**Scenario.** Rolling updates and `docker compose down` are slow; the application logs no shutdown message.

**Symptoms.** `docker stop` takes about 10 seconds; the exit code is 137; the shutdown hook output is missing.

**Diagnosis.** `docker top NAME` or `docker exec NAME ps -e` shows a shell or wrapper script as PID 1 with the application as its child (second case in the experiment above).

**Root cause.** The shell did not forward SIGTERM and, as PID 1 without a handler, ignored it; after the timeout the daemon sent SIGKILL.

**Fix.** Use the exec form of `ENTRYPOINT`, end wrapper scripts with `exec`, or run with `--init`. Make the application handle SIGTERM (in Spring Boot, graceful shutdown, described in the next chapter).

**Prevention.** Add a check to the pipeline: start the image, run `docker stop`, assert the duration is below a few seconds and the exit code is 143 or 0.

#### Problem 9: build is slow because every change re-downloads dependencies

This is the cache-order problem treated in the previous chapter; the Dockerfile-level remedy is to copy `pom.xml` and run `mvn dependency:go-offline` (or the build with a BuildKit cache mount for `~/.m2`) before copying `src`. A `.dockerignore` file listing `target/` and `.git` removes a second cause, in which build output copied into the context invalidates `COPY .` `.`.

### Questions to expect

**Q1. What is the difference between CMD and ENTRYPOINT?** ENTRYPOINT defines the executable that always runs; CMD provides default arguments that can be replaced on the `docker run` command line. Without ENTRYPOINT, CMD is the whole default command. Arguments given to `docker run IMAGE ARGS` replace CMD and are appended to ENTRYPOINT.

**Q2. Why prefer the exec form?** The program is started directly as PID 1 and receives signals. In the shell form `/bin/sh -c` is PID 1 and may not forward SIGTERM; variable expansion works only in the shell form.

**Q3. What is the difference between COPY and ADD?** COPY copies files; ADD additionally extracts local tar archives and downloads URLs. COPY is preferred because it is explicit.

**Q4. What is the difference between ENV and ARG?** ARG is available only at build time and is not present in running containers; ENV persists in the image and in containers. Neither is suitable for secrets, because both are visible in image metadata or the process environment.

**Q5. What does EXPOSE do?** It records the port in the image metadata as documentation (and for `docker run -P`). It does not publish the port. **Q6. Why must a Dockerfile order its instructions carefully?** The cache invalidates from the first changed step. Dependencies that change rarely should be installed before frequently changing source is copied.

**Q7. What is a multi-stage build and why is it used?** Several FROM stages in one Dockerfile; only selected files are copied into the final stage. It keeps build tools out of the runtime image, reducing size and attack surface.

**Q8. What does a HEALTHCHECK do and what does it not do?** It runs a command periodically and records healthy or unhealthy. The daemon does not restart the container; Compose conditions and orchestrators use the status.

**Q9. Why use** `.dockerignore`**?** To shrink the build context, avoid leaking files such as `.env` or `.git` and prevent unrelated changes from invalidating the cache.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Order instructions from stable to volatile and combine commands that must share a layer.
- Use the exec form for ENTRYPOINT, make the application PID 1 (or use exec/--init) and handle SIGTERM.
- Set a numeric non-root USER, a HEALTHCHECK that the image can actually execute and a .dockerignore.
- ARG is build-time only and ENV is runtime; neither is a secret store.
- Multi-stage builds cut size by an order of magnitude in the measured examples (283 MB to 1.14 MB, 335 MB to 95.3 MB).

A Spring Boot application packaged as an executable (fat) jar can be placed in an image with two lines, but the result is a poor image: one large layer that changes on every build, a JVM that may size its heap incorrectly, a process that may ignore termination signals and a configuration approach that bakes environment details into the image. This chapter assembles an image for `orders-service` that avoids these problems and compares the three common ways to build it: a hand-written Dockerfile, Cloud Native Buildpacks and Jib.

The JVM behaviours (container-aware heap sizing, OOM kill, SIGTERM handling) were measured with the `orders-service-lite` image, which runs on the same JVM (OpenJDK 21.0.12) under the same cgroup limits.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Fat jar compared with layered jar

An executable Spring Boot jar contains application classes, all dependency jars and a loader. Copied as a single file it forms one layer. Because the dependencies change rarely and the application classes change on every commit, a single-layer image re-transfers hundreds of megabytes of unchanged libraries on each push and pull.

Spring Boot supports **layered jars**. The jar contains an index (`layers.idx`) that assigns each entry to one of four layers: `dependencies`, `spring-boot-loader`, `snapshot-dependencies` and `application`. Per the Spring Boot reference (Dockerfiles page, consulted October 2026, documentation of release 4.1.1; releases 3.3 to 3.5 have equivalent pages), the layers are extracted with the `tools` jar mode and copied into the image one layer per `COPY`:

blocks.code:
$ java -Djarmode=tools -jar application.jar extract --layers --destination extracted
$ java -Djarmode=tools -jar application.jar list-layers
blocks.title: Extraction command (illustrative, not run)

blocks.text: The older `layertools` mode is the predecessor of `tools`; from memory it was deprecated in favour of `tools`, so verify the mode available in the Spring Boot version in use.

#### The JVM inside a container

The JVM reads the container limits from the cgroup (container support is on by default; the option is `-XX:+UseContainerSupport`). The maximum heap defaults to a fraction of the memory limit: `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage` (default 25) and, for small memory, `-XX:MinRAMPercentage` (default 50, used when the limit is small). The number of CPUs seen by the JVM follows the `--cpus` quota. Measured on the build machine with the demonstration image (reported by `Runtime.maxMemory()`):

blocks.caption: Default heap sizing observed under limits.

blocks.text: The heap is only a part of the process memory: metaspace, thread stacks, the code cache, direct buffers and garbage collector structures also count against the container limit. Setting the heap equal to the limit (or `-Xmx` larger than the limit) therefore invites the kernel OOM killer.

blocks.text:
#### Base images

The runtime image needs a JRE (or a JDK only when the application compiles code at run time). Common choices, from memory (verify the current tags): `eclipse-temurin:21-jre` (Debian or Ubuntu based, includes a shell and a package manager), `eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine` (musl libc, small), and `gcr.io/distroless/java21-debian12` (no shell, no package manager). Alpine uses musl instead of glibc: most pure-Java applications run unchanged, but native libraries compiled for glibc (some JNI drivers, profilers, certain DNS behaviour) can fail. Distroless images reduce attack surface but offer no shell for `docker exec` debugging, so a debug variant or an ephemeral debug container is needed. Whatever the choice, pin a specific tag or digest and rebuild regularly to receive security fixes.

### Worked example

#### Memory limits and the OOM killer with a JVM

Two containers were started with `--memory 128m --memory-swap 128m` and 150 MB then 300 MB of heap were requested through `/alloc`. The helper `alloc.sh` runs `docker exec NAME bash -c` with a request to `/alloc?mb=N` sent through bash `/dev/tcp`, because the image has no curl.

blocks.code:
$ docker run -d --name v2-oomA --memory 128m --memory-swap 128m v2-orders:1
$ docker logs v2-oomA | head -1
max heap MiB = 61, cpus = 2, db = jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/orders
$ ./alloc.sh v2-oomA 150
$ docker inspect -f 'status={{.State.Status}} OOMKilled={{.State.OOMKilled}} \
    exit={{.State.ExitCode}}' v2-oomA
status=running OOMKilled=false exit=0
$ docker logs v2-oomA 2>&1 | grep -m1 Exception
Exception in thread "pool-1-thread-1" java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space
blocks.title: Default heap sizing: the JVM protects itself

blocks.text: The maximum heap (61 MiB) was below the limit, so the request thread failed with `OutOfMemoryError` and the container stayed up. With an explicit heap larger than the container:

blocks.code:
$ docker run -d --name v2-oomB --memory 128m --memory-swap 128m \
    -e JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS=-Xmx400m v2-orders:1
$ ./alloc.sh v2-oomB 300
$ docker inspect -f 'status={{.State.Status}} OOMKilled={{.State.OOMKilled}} \
    exit={{.State.ExitCode}}' v2-oomB
status=exited OOMKilled=true exit=137
blocks.title: Heap larger than the container: kernel kill

blocks.text:
The JVM accepted `-Xmx400m` because it did not know the cgroup limit would be reached, and the kernel killed the process at 128 MiB. The environment variable `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` is read by every JVM and is a convenient way to set flags without changing the `ENTRYPOINT`; the JVM prints `Picked up JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS: ...` on start.

#### Graceful shutdown

Kubernetes, Compose and `docker stop` all begin termination with SIGTERM. A Spring Boot application should stop accepting new requests, finish in-flight requests and close resources before exiting. Two properties control it:

blocks.code:
server.shutdown=graceful
spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase=20s
blocks.title: application.properties

blocks.text:
Per the Spring Boot reference (graceful shutdown page, consulted October 2026), graceful shutdown allows existing requests to complete during a grace period while new requests are refused. The same page states that graceful is the default in the documented release; older 3.x releases defaulted to `immediate`, from memory, so setting the property explicitly is advisable. The default timeout of 30 seconds is also from memory. The grace period must be shorter than the stop timeout of the platform (10 s for `docker stop` unless `-t` or `stop_grace_period` is set; 30 s for a Kubernetes pod by default). The demonstration image exercises the same mechanism (a JVM shutdown hook) and stopped in 0.1 s with exit code 143 when it was PID 1.

#### Illustrative Dockerfile for orders-service (not run)

The following Dockerfile builds the layered image in three stages. It was not built on the build machine because Maven cannot download dependencies there; its structure mirrors the stages that were built for the demonstration image. Image names are those documented as available on Docker Hub (from memory, verify before use).

blocks.code:
# illustrative configuration (not run)
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk AS build
WORKDIR /workspace
COPY .mvn/ .mvn/
COPY mvnw pom.xml ./
RUN ./mvnw -B -q dependency:go-offline
COPY src/ src/
RUN ./mvnw -B -q -DskipTests package \
 && cp target/orders-service-*.jar application.jar

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk AS extract
WORKDIR /extract
COPY --from=build /workspace/application.jar .
RUN java -Djarmode=tools -jar application.jar extract --layers --destination extracted

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
RUN useradd --uid 10001 --no-create-home --shell /usr/sbin/nologin orders
WORKDIR /application
COPY --from=extract /extract/extracted/dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=extract /extract/extracted/spring-boot-loader/ ./
COPY --from=extract /extract/extracted/snapshot-dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=extract /extract/extracted/application/ ./
ENV JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75"
EXPOSE 8080
USER 10001
HEALTHCHECK --interval=15s --timeout=3s --start-period=40s --retries=3 \
  CMD ["java", "-cp", "/application/application.jar", "-version"]
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "application.jar"]
blocks.title: Dockerfile

blocks.text:
What to notice: the dependency resolution step (`go-offline`) depends only on `pom.xml`, so it stays cached while sources change; the final `COPY` instructions are ordered from the most stable to the most volatile layer; `ENTRYPOINT` `["java", "-jar", "application.jar"]` follows the Spring Boot reference for the extracted layout (the launcher jar contains only application code and references the extracted libraries). The `HEALTHCHECK` shown is a placeholder: a JRE image usually lacks `curl`, so a real probe uses `wget` or a small Java client, or the health check is defined in Compose or Kubernetes (where the platform calls `/actuator/health`). The `.dockerignore` must exclude `target/` and `.git`.

#### Configuration through environment variables

Spring Boot maps environment variables to properties by relaxed binding: `SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL` sets `spring.datasource.url`, `SERVER_PORT` sets `server.port`. The image therefore contains no environment-specific values; the platform injects them:

blocks.code:
$ docker run -d --name orders --network backend \
    -e SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL=jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/orders \
    -e SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME=orders_app \
    -e SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD_FILE=/run/secrets/db_password \
    -p 8080:8080 orders-service:1.4.2
blocks.title: Run with environment-specific configuration (illustrative, not run)

blocks.text:
The `_FILE` variable is not a Spring Boot feature by default; secrets mounted as files are read by a `spring.config.import=configtree:/run/secrets/` setting (from memory, verify) or by the platform. Passwords in plain environment variables are visible in `docker inspect` and `/proc/PID/environ`, which is why the security chapters recommend secret stores.

#### Health checks through the actuator

With `spring-boot-starter-actuator`, the endpoint `/actuator/health` reports `{"status":"UP"}` when all health indicators are up, including the database. Per the Spring Boot reference (consulted October 2026), liveness and readiness state indicators are available and the property `management.endpoint.health.probes.enabled` defaults to `true`; the paths `/actuator/health/liveness` and `/actuator/health/readiness` are from memory and are verified in the Kubernetes chapter. Keep the database in readiness, not in liveness: restarting the application does not repair a database outage.

*Three ways to build the orders-service image (from the Spring Boot and tool documentation; verify versions).*

The Spring Boot Maven plugin goal `spring-boot:build-image` uses a Paketo builder image and pulls it from a registry on first use (the default image name derives from the project coordinates, per the Spring Boot documentation, consulted October 2026). None of the three commands could be run on the build machine.

### Hands-on

Objective: observe how container limits change JVM sizing.

1. Build or obtain any image with a JVM (for example the `eclipse-temurin:21-jre` image).
2. Run `docker run --rm IMAGE java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep -E` `"MaxHeapSize|MaxRAMPercentage|UseContainerSupport"` without a limit, then with `--memory 512m` and `--memory` `256m`.
3. Compute `MaxHeapSize` divided by the limit in each case.
4. Add `-e JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS=-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75` and repeat.
5. Start a Spring Boot application with `docker run --memory 300m -e JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS=-Xmx600m ...` and generate load to see exit code 137 after the heap grows.

Expected result: about 25 percent of the limit by default (50 percent for very small limits), the configured percentage when set, and OOMKilled when `-Xmx` exceeds the limit.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem 10: the JVM container is OOMKilled although the heap looks fine

**Scenario.** `orders-service` runs with `--memory 512m` and a fixed `-Xmx512m`. After some hours of traffic the container restarts.

**Symptoms.** Exit code 137 with `OOMKilled=true`; no `OutOfMemoryError` in the log; heap graphs show usage below the maximum.

**Diagnosis.** Compare the container limit with the sum of heap, metaspace, thread stacks, code cache and direct buffers. `docker stats` shows memory use near the limit. In the experiment above, an `-Xmx` larger than the limit gave `OOMKilled=true`.

**Root cause.** The heap alone was allowed to use the entire limit, so the non-heap memory pushed the process over it and the kernel killed it before the JVM could raise an error.

**Fix.** Use `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=60` to `75` and keep the limit higher than the heap by the expected non-heap amount; reduce thread counts and direct buffer use if needed.

**Prevention.** Load test with production limits and alert on restarts with reason `OOMKilled`.

#### Problem 11: JVM sees all host CPUs and memory

**Scenario.** An older base image or JVM is run with limits and sizes its thread pools from the host's CPU count.

**Symptoms.** Many GC and compiler threads, high throttling, heap far larger than the limit.

**Diagnosis.** Print `Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors()` and `maxMemory()` at start (the demonstration application does so: `cpus = 1` under `--cpus 1`, `max heap MiB = 2008` without a limit). Check `java` `-XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep UseContainerSupport`.

**Root cause.** JVMs before the container-support backports (Java 8 releases before 8u191) read the host values. Java 21 reads the cgroup.

**Fix.** Use a current JVM (Java 21 here), set `-XX:ActiveProcessorCount` only when necessary and set the memory limits explicitly.

**Prevention.** Log the detected values at start-up in every environment.

#### Problem 12: certificates, time zone and locale missing in a slim image

**Scenario.** The application works in the full image and fails in a minimal one.

**Symptoms.** `PKIX path building failed` or `unable to find valid certification path` on HTTPS calls; timestamps in UTC although `TZ` is set; garbled characters. **Diagnosis.** On the build machine, the stripped image has no certificate store, no zoneinfo and no locale files. `date` with `TZ=Asia/Kolkata` printed the abbreviation `Asia` and the UTC time, because the zone database was absent:

blocks.code:
$ docker run --rm -e TZ=Asia/Kolkata v2-base:1 date
Tue Oct 20 03:15:18 Asia 2026
$ docker run --rm v2-jre:21 bash -c 'ls /etc/ssl/certs; ls /usr/share/zoneinfo'
ls: cannot access '/etc/ssl/certs': No such file or directory
ls: cannot access '/usr/share/zoneinfo': No such file or directory
blocks.title: Missing zone database (observed)

blocks.text:
**Root cause.** Minimal images omit the `ca-certificates` and `tzdata` packages and locale data. The JDK has its own time-zone data and its own trust store (`lib/security/cacerts`), so Java is affected by the trust store but not by the OS zone database; native tools and glibc functions are affected by both.

**Fix.** Install the packages in the image (`ca-certificates`, `tzdata`) or use a base image that includes them, and set `-Duser.timezone` or `TZ` explicitly. For Java, confirm that `cacerts` exists in the runtime image; a runtime created with `jlink` must contain it.

**Prevention.** Include an HTTPS call and a time-zone assertion in the smoke test of the image.

### Questions to expect

**Q1. Why is a layered jar better than a fat jar in an image?** The layers separate stable dependencies from frequently changing application classes. A code change invalidates only the top layer, so builds, pushes and pulls transfer a few kilobytes instead of the whole jar.

**Q2. How does the JVM decide its heap size in a container?** With container support it reads the cgroup memory limit and uses `MaxRAMPercentage` (default 25) of it, with a larger fraction for very small limits. The flag `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage` changes the fraction.

**Q3. Why should** `-Xmx` **not equal the container memory limit?** Heap is only part of the process memory. Metaspace, stacks, code cache and native buffers add to it, and exceeding the cgroup limit gets the process SIGKILLed (exit 137) without a Java exception.

**Q4. What does exit code 137 mean for a Java container?** The process was killed by SIGKILL, commonly the kernel OOM killer (`OOMKilled=true`) or `docker stop` after its timeout. Exit code 143 means SIGTERM was handled.

**Q5. How is graceful shutdown configured in Spring Boot?** `server.shutdown=graceful` and `spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase`. The JVM must receive SIGTERM, so it has to be PID 1 or started with exec.

**Q6. Compare buildpacks, Jib and a Dockerfile.** A Dockerfile gives full control and requires maintenance. Buildpacks (`spring-boot:build-image`) build a layered image with a standard builder and require a Docker daemon. Jib builds from Maven or Gradle without a Dockerfile and, for `jib:build`, without a daemon.

**Q7. How is configuration passed to a containerised Spring Boot application?** Through environment variables (relaxed binding, for example `SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL`), mounted config files or a config server; secrets from a secret store. The image stays environment-independent.

**Q8. When is Alpine a poor choice for Java?** When native libraries built for glibc are used, or when subtle musl differences (DNS resolution, locale) cause issues. Debian-based or distroless images avoid these at the cost of size.

**Q9. Why include the database in readiness but not liveness?** Liveness failures restart the container, which does not repair an external outage; readiness only removes the instance from traffic.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Use a layered jar (jarmode tools) so that dependency layers stay cached and only the application layer changes.
- Under limits the JVM sizes the heap as a fraction of the cgroup limit (25 percent by default); set MaxRAMPercentage deliberately and never let heap equal the limit.
- A heap above the container limit gives OOMKilled and exit 137; a heap below it gives OutOfMemoryError inside a running container.
- SIGTERM must reach the JVM (exec form, PID 1) and Spring Boot should shut down gracefully.
- Dockerfile, buildpacks and Jib all produce OCI images; choose by control, daemon availability and maintenance cost.
- Minimal images may lack CA certificates, time-zone data and locales; test for them.

An application such as `orders-service` consists of several containers: the service, a PostgreSQL database and, optionally, a cache. Starting them with separate `docker run` commands requires the reader to remember networks, volumes, environment variables and start order. **Docker Compose** describes the whole stack in one YAML file (`compose.yaml`) and starts, stops and inspects it with one command. Compose is used for local development, for integration tests in a pipeline and for small single-host deployments; production clusters use an orchestrator (see the Kubernetes chapters).

### Concept and mechanism

A Compose file follows the Compose Specification. The top-level keys are `services`, `networks`, `volumes`, `configs`, `secrets` and `name`. The obsolete `version:` key is not needed in current Compose (a warning is printed if it is present; from memory, verify against the current specification). The tool is invoked as `docker compose` (a plugin of the Docker CLI; version v5.5.1 on the build machine).

#### Start order and readiness

`depends_on` controls the order of creation and removal. By default it waits only until the dependency container is *running*. Per the Docker documentation (startup order page, consulted October 2026) the available conditions are `service_started`, `service_healthy` (the dependency's healthcheck must pass) and `service_completed_successfully` (the dependency must run to completion, suited to migration jobs). A running database is not yet a database that accepts connections, so applications that connect at start-up need `service_healthy`.

#### Profiles, override files and variables

A service with `profiles: ["cache"]` is ignored unless `--profile cache` (or `COMPOSE_PROFILES`) is given. Compose reads `compose.yaml` and, when present, `compose.override.yaml` and merges them: maps are merged key by key, so the override file adds development settings (debug logging, extra ports, bind mounts) without touching the base file. More files can be combined with repeated `-f`. A `.env` file next to the compose file supplies values for `${VARIABLE}` substitution; `${VAR:?message}` makes the variable mandatory and `${VAR:-default}` supplies a default. Secrets must not be committed: `.env` belongs in `.gitignore` and in `.dockerignore`.

### Worked example

#### The compose.yaml for orders-service

The file below describes `orders-service`, PostgreSQL and an optional Redis cache. Image names are parameters so that the same file runs with locally built images (on the build machine the two variables point to the demonstration images; the real `postgres:16` and `redis:7` cannot be pulled there).

blocks.code:
name: orders

services:
  db:
    image: ${POSTGRES_IMAGE:-postgres:16}
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: orders_app
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD:?set DB_PASSWORD in .env}
      POSTGRES_DB: orders
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "pg_isready", "-U", "orders_app", "-d", "orders"]
      interval: 3s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 10
    networks:
      - backend

  orders-service:
    image: ${ORDERS_IMAGE:-orders-service:dev}
    build:
      context: .
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
    environment:
      SERVER_PORT: "8080"
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL: jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/orders
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME: orders_app
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD}
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "/app/healthcheck.sh"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 5
      start_period: 5s
    restart: unless-stopped
    networks:
      - backend

  redis:
    image: redis:7
    profiles: ["cache"]
    networks:
      - backend

volumes:
  pgdata:

networks:
  backend:

#### Running the stack

The project name was set to `v2orders` with `-p` so that all objects carry the `v2` prefix.

$ export POSTGRES_IMAGE=v2-postgres:16 ORDERS_IMAGE=v2-orders:1
$ docker compose -p v2orders config --services
db
orders-service
$ docker compose -p v2orders --profile cache config --services
db
orders-service
redis

The application container started only after `Healthy` was reported for the database, and its own health status became `healthy` because the TCP check against `db:5432` succeeded. The host `curl` worked through the published port (the userland proxy, see the networking chapter).

#### Start order without the health condition

An override file (the `!override` tag is a Compose extension, so the listing is shown as plain text and is not parsed by standard YAML loaders) replaced the dependency with the short form (`depends_on: !override [db]`, which waits only for the container to run) and delayed the database by 8 seconds to imitate a slow start:

**compose.race.yaml**

blocks.code:
services:
  db:
    entrypoint: ["bash", "-c", "sleep 8; exec /usr/local/bin/entrypoint.sh"]
  orders-service:
    depends_on: !override
      - db

$ docker compose -p v2orders -f compose.yaml -f compose.race.yaml up -d --no-build --pull never
 Container v2orders-db-1 Started
 Container v2orders-orders-service-1 Started
$ sleep 4; ./probe.sh        # t+4 s
{"status":"DOWN","db":"unreachable db"}
$ sleep 10; ./probe.sh       # t+14 s
{"status":"UP"}
blocks.title: The race and its resolution

blocks.text:
Both containers started immediately, and the application reported `DOWN` while the database was initialising. The demonstration application polls the database on every health request and therefore recovers. A Spring Boot application that opens its connection pool at start-up would fail the start (typically with a `Connection refused` stack trace) and, with `restart: unless-stopped`, loop until the database is ready. With `service_healthy` the first Compose output above had no such window.

Persistence behaviour of `down` and `down -v` is covered with real output in the chapter on runtime and storage.

#### Compose for development and integration tests

For development, `compose.override.yaml` adds bind mounts of the source tree, a debug port and verbose logging without changing the base file. For integration tests in a pipeline, `docker compose up -d --wait` (waits for the services to be running or healthy; from memory, verify) starts the stack, tests run against `localhost:8080`, and `docker compose` `down -v` removes containers, network and volumes so that every run starts clean. In Java tests, **Testcontainers** starts the same kind of throwaway containers from test code (for example a `PostgreSQLContainer`); see the Spring Boot testing material. Compose suits end-to-end checks of the packaged image, Testcontainers suits tests that need a database inside the JVM test lifecycle.

### Hands-on

Objective: run the stack and observe start-order behaviour.

1. Create a directory with the `compose.yaml` above (use real images `postgres:16`, and for the application any image that exposes port 8080 and a `/actuator/health` endpoint, for example the image built in the Dockerfile chapter) and a `.env` file with `DB_PASSWORD=local-only`.
2. Run `docker compose config` and confirm that the variables were substituted.
3. Run `docker compose up -d`, then `docker compose ps` until both services are healthy.
4. Run `docker compose exec db psql -U orders_app -d orders -c 'select 1'`.
5. Replace the dependency condition by the short form `depends_on: [db]`, run `docker compose down` and `up -d`, and observe whether the application logs connection errors during start-up.
6. Remove everything with `docker compose down -v`.

Expected result: substituted values in step 2, both services healthy in step 3, and (depending on database speed) connection errors in step 5 that disappear with `service_healthy`.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem 18: the application starts before the database is ready

**Scenario.** After `docker compose up` the `orders-service` container exits or reports errors while the database is still initialising.

**Symptoms.** `Connection refused` or `the database system is starting up` in the application log, followed by restarts.

**Diagnosis.** `docker compose ps` shows the database `starting` (not `healthy`) when the application starts. The experiment above reproduced it: the health endpoint returned `{"status":"DOWN","db":"unreachable db"}` at 4 seconds.

**Root cause.** `depends_on` without a condition waits only for the container to run. A database process that is running is not yet accepting connections.

**Fix.** Add a `healthcheck` to the database (`pg_isready`) and `depends_on: db: condition: service_healthy`. In addition, configure connection retries in the application (HikariCP `initializationFailTimeout`, Spring Retry) so that the service survives a database restart later.

**Prevention.** Treat start order as a readiness problem rather than a sequencing problem, in Compose and in Kubernetes alike.

#### Problem 19: every developer has a different configuration

**Scenario.** The stack works for one developer and fails for another with `variable is not set` or wrong ports.

**Symptoms.** A warning that `DB_PASSWORD` is not set, or a port conflict on 8080.

**Diagnosis.** `docker compose config` prints the effective, substituted file and shows which values were used and which files were merged.

**Root cause.** Environment-specific values were taken from the developer's shell or from an untracked `.env` that differs between machines.

**Fix.** Commit an `.env.example` with names and harmless defaults, use `${VAR:?message}` for mandatory values and `${VAR:-default}` for optional ones, and keep personal changes in `compose.override.yaml`.

**Prevention.** Run `docker compose config` in the pipeline to detect unresolved variables.

### Questions to expect

**Q1. What problem does Docker Compose solve?** It defines a multi-container application (services, networks, volumes, configuration) in one file and manages it with single commands, making local and test environments reproducible.

**Q2. How do services find each other in Compose?** Compose creates a user-defined network and registers each service name in the embedded DNS, so `jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/orders` resolves.

**Q3. What does** `depends_on` **guarantee?** Start (and stop) order. By default only that the dependency container is running. With `condition: service_healthy` the dependency must also pass its healthcheck; `service_completed_successfully` waits for a job to finish.

**Q4. What are profiles?** A way to mark optional services (for example a cache or debugging tools) that start only when the profile is activated.

**Q5. How are environment-specific values supplied?** Through `environment`, `env_file`, `${VAR}` substitution from the shell or `.env`, and override files.

**Q6. What is** `compose.override.yaml`**?** A file merged automatically over `compose.yaml`, used for development settings. Other combinations are chosen with `-f`.

**Q7. What is the difference between** `down` **and** `down -v`**?** `down` removes containers and networks but keeps named volumes; `-v` also removes the volumes and therefore the data.

**Q8. Compose or Testcontainers for integration tests?** Compose starts the packaged stack from outside the code and suits end-to-end tests; Testcontainers starts containers from test code and suits tests inside the build.

**Q9. Is Compose suitable for production?** Acceptable for a single host with modest availability needs; it lacks multi-host scheduling, rolling updates and self-healing across nodes, which orchestrators provide.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- One compose.yaml describes services, networks and volumes; services reach each other by service name.
- Use healthchecks with depends\_on condition service\_healthy; plain depends\_on only orders container start.
- Keep secrets out of the file: variables with ${VAR:?}, an untracked .env, override files for local changes.
- docker compose config shows the effective result; down keeps volumes, down -v deletes them.
- Compose suits development, integration tests and single-host setups.

A container shares the host kernel, runs as root by default and contains whatever the image builder put into its layers. Three kinds of weakness follow: secrets baked into layers that anyone with the image can read, containers that grant an attacker more power than the application needs, and access to the Docker daemon, which is equivalent to root on the host. This chapter demonstrates each with commands and lists the controls that reduce the risk.
